title: Candidate creation-story probing notes
notes:
Purpose: quick, noisy synthesis to help prep for follow-up interview and hiring panel. Mostly thinking aloud / prompts to use in next conversation. Not polished — keep it ephemeral.

Quick gist: Candidate (Eddie Yu — PM-level infra engineer) has strong surface-level signals: articulate, shipped systems at small orgs, clear latency/cost instincts. Some claims around "we replaced the cache layer and saved 30%" need concrete follow-up. He describes ownership of a deployment orchestration piece that sounds like our autoscaler work but could be narrower.

Objective for follow-up: force concrete decomposition of the work they led -> technical decisions, tradeoffs, failure modes, and what they would change if given more time/resources. Use combination of timeline reconstruction + targeted hypotheticals.

Timeline reconstruction probes (walk them through 6-12 month arc):
- "Start to finish: what was the initial problem statement your team committed to? Who wrote it? What metrics were you tracking?"
- "Show me the first design sketch you drew (even rough). How did that evolve after the first test?"
- "Three forks in the road you explicitly considered and why you rejected them — be specific about performance/cost/operational burden tradeoffs."
- "Tell me about the deployment cadence: how did you ship changes safely? How did you rollback? Any incidents tied to rollout?"

Decision-detail probes (ask for numbers, not handwavy statements):
- "When you say 'reduced latency by 20–30%', what was the exact p95/p99 before/after and how long did the improvement persist?"
- "How did you measure tail latency — synthetic load vs real traffic? Sampling frequency?"
- "What was the distribution of sequence lengths / request sizes you optimized for? Any bucketing/segmentation?"
- "What kernels/ops were the bottleneck and how did you confirm? Profilers / flamegraphs / perf events?"

Operational rigor signals to probe:
- Incident root cause: "Give me the incident timeline for the worst outage — detection, mitigation, RCA, and specific follow-up actions. Which actions were automated vs manual?"
- Monitoring: "What dashboards/alerts did you own? How many false positives did you tolerate? Any alert fatigue tradeoffs you explicitly managed?"
- Ownership boundaries: "Which parts of the stack were out of scope for your team and how did you coordinate cross-team changes?"

Quality-of-thought hypotheticals (fast calibrators):
- "Imagine the model size doubles and p99 SLA stays the same. Walk me through 5 immediate changes you would consider across infra, model slicing, and customer routing."
- "If you could make one irreversible change to the product runtime, what would you pick and why?"

Red flags to watch for during follow-up (stop-gap heuristics):
- Vague answers to 'how' (prefers product-sounding narratives without ops/metrics)
- Can't name specific profiling evidence or tests that validated a hypothesis
- Over-reliance on third-party services without concrete failure handling ("we relied on X managed cache and it always worked")
- Evades discussion about rollback/incident follow-through

Positive signals we want to confirm:
- Mentions of small, measurable experiments with clear metrics and short feedback loops
- Ownership of cross-cutting changes (example: coordinated kernel change + config rollout + canary gating)
- Clear understanding of tail behavior and cost tradeoffs (prefix caching, batching strategies, quantization choices)

Suggested follow-ups / exercises for next interview:
- 20–30 minute whiteboard: sketch an autoscaler that optimizes cost while preserving p95 SLA. Ask for data inputs, control loop, and failure modes. Push on how they'd test it.
- Take-home micro: 2–3 short prompts: (1) given a sample perf profile, identify top 3 hotspots and prioritize fixes; (2) write a short design note (1 page) for a cache invalidation strategy across regionally routed inferences.

Panel alignment notes (how I'd pitch to the panel):
- Strength: practical bias for measurable experiments and awareness of tail metrics.
- Risk: tends to describe things at team/process level; need to validate low-level perf fluency and incident discipline.
- Recommendation for vote: request follow-up technical deep-dive + invite infra-sw engineer to pair on whiteboard.

Notes-to-self (specific asks during follow-up):
- Ask for exact p95/p99 numbers and load profile (QPS, concurrency, typical sequence length).
- Ask them to demo a perf report or flamegraph if available (even if redacted).
- Ask for a short narrative of one incident where their change made things worse before it made things better — what did they learn?

Loose scorecard (quick, noisy):
- System design thinking: 7/10
- Low-level perf debug: 5/10 (so far, unknown)
- Ownership & cross-team coordination: 8/10
- Incident response & SRE hygiene: 5/10
- Recommendation: follow-up + partial onsite focused on perf/ops replication

Unresolved open questions for hiring thread:
- Did they author any automation or infra-as-code that we can read? Repo links?
- How much of their claims are individual vs team accomplishments?
- Evidence of continuous testing for performance regressions?

Action items after follow-up:
- If follow-up satisfies perf fluency, prepare a short take-home pair on real perf artifact (30–40m).
- If follow-up remains fuzzy, escalate to "no hire" or consider senior engineer role with strong mentoring plan (depends on panel).

Random shorthand and cues to use in convo: 
- "Show me the raw numbers"
- "Walk me through your flamegraph"
- "What failed first when you increased load"
- "How did you know the fix was safe to roll out?"

End of notes. Repeat after convo: move to candidate-card (INF hiring board) with precise p95/p99, repo links, incident timeline in comments.
